Business-development / rainmaking toolkit: personal referral network, relationship-nurturing, lead follow-up and close (the firm supplies 'training and coaching' to expand it)
A CRM / pipeline for tracking self-sourced client leads (implied, not named)
The firm's bench of C-suite consultants (CFO/COO/CMO/CHRO/CIO/CTO) and strategic-alliance partner firms, assembled into client engagement teams
Diagnostic / discovery skills — peer-level CEO conversations to isolate an organization's core issues
JazzHR (the ATS the posting itself runs on — a recruiting-funnel signal, not a delivery tool)

No codebase or technical stack — and none is expected for this role

Engage owners/CEOs at a peer level — listen, ask the right questions, and determine the core issues before prescribing solutions

statedVsRealGaps: Title vs. structure: the posting reads 'Chief Executive Officer,' but this is not an employed CEO seat — it's an independent principal/consultant role. 'No buy-in or startup fees,' 'retain [%] of revenues billed to clients,' and the 'entrepreneurial spirit' language describe a 1099, eat-what-you-kill arrangement, not a salaried executive job.

Delivery vs. sales: the title implies pure executive expertise, but the responsibilities lean heavily on business development — 'help to close leads for new clients.' Real income depends on self-sourcing and closing your own client book, not just CEO craft.

Comp is under-specified: the revenue-share percentage is literally blank in the posting, and benefits are framed as 'access to' a Cigna plan — likely self-funded group access rather than employer-paid coverage. Easy to misread as a traditional benefits package.

Light gate vs. broad promise: requirements are modest (bachelor's, 5+ years as a CEO/owner) against a promise to deliver 'the best solutions to our clients across the globe.' The screening bar is thin relative to the positioning.

Asserted but unspecified IP: the 'tools, training and coaching' and the 'strategic alliance' network are repeatedly cited as differentiators but never defined — no methodology, deliverable format, or proprietary asset is described.

'Powered by JazzHR' plus generic, repetitive copy points to a high-volume templated recruiting funnel — consistent with a network/affiliate model that onboards many consultants, not a selective single hire.
riskAreas: Income risk: compensation is effectively revenue-share with no base and no client book provided — earnings hinge entirely on the consultant's own ability to source and close engagements.
Expectation mismatch: candidates drawn by the 'CEO' title may expect an executive salary and seat and instead find a self-employed, BD-heavy fractional gig.
Brand/quality control: a thin qualification bar combined with an ATS-driven, high-volume intake risks variable consultant quality and reputational dilution for clients.
Benefits ambiguity: 'access to' insurance and unspecified 'discounts' may be self-paid; the blank revenue percentage leaves the core economic term undefined.

Thin specification: success metrics, engagement model, scope of firm-provided 'tools/training,' and how alliance teams are staffed/compensated are all unstated — hard to assess fit or upside without follow-up.
Global-delivery promise vs. solo-operator reality: 'clients across the globe' sits oddly against a model where each principal largely runs their own practice.
analysis.reflection: Stated as a 'Consulting CEO,' the real body of work is two roles fused: a genuinely high-skill advisory practice (peer-level diagnosis, turnarounds, scaling, executive coaching, assembling cross-functional teams) and an independent business-development practice where you must find, nurture, and close your own clients. The strongest, most specific signals in the JD are commercial, not executive — 'no buy-in fees,' 'retain [%] of revenues,' 'help to close leads,' 'entrepreneurial spirit' — which together describe a 1099 principal in an affiliate-style network rather than an employed chief executive. The advisory demands themselves are real and high; the role's weakness is specification, not substance: the revenue split is blank, benefits are 'access to,' and the firm's differentiating 'tools and training' are asserted but never described. A strong fit is a seasoned operator-CEO who is also a natural rainmaker and comfortable with variable, self-generated income; a poor fit is someone reading the title as a salaried executive post. There is no codebase and none is expected — this is correctly judged in the role's own consulting terms.

case.title: Fractional CEO Engagement: Diagnose, Scope, and Win the 'Meridian Tooling' Account
case.brief: A referral has landed in the firm's pipeline. Dana Brandt is the owner-CEO of Meridian Tooling Co., a ~$18M, 42-person family-owned B2B industrial-components business that has 'stopped growing,' and a mutual contact suggested she talk to you. You have had one 35-minute discovery call (transcript supplied) and Dana has sent a follow-up email asking 'what working together would look like.' This case is the work you would actually do between that first call and winning (or walking away from) the engagement: read the situation at a peer level, isolate the core issues before prescribing anything, design an engagement and a team for it, and convert the lead on terms that work for both Dana and the firm's revenue-share model. The starting materials are deliberately incomplete and partly self-contradictory — that is what a real first look is like; treat surfacing the gaps as part of the job, not a failure of the brief. The provided materials fit this role directly (no synthetic substitution was needed). Budget ~2 hours total. Throughout, keep a short DECISIONS log (Task 4) — this is normal engagement hygiene at the firm, the record a principal hands to the bench team they pull in, not a test artifact. We care far more about your judgment and the path you take through the ambiguity than about polish or volume; one tight page per deliverable beats five padded ones.
case.repoSeed:
A prospective-client packet (the firm's standard 'Discovery folder' for an open pipeline card), drawing on your personal playbooks (turnaround, scaling, executive coaching, team-building), the firm's bench, and the CRM:
- discovery_call_transcript.md — lightly edited transcript of your first 35-minute call with owner-CEO Dana Brandt. Dana's framing throughout: 'we've plateaued, I think we have a sales and marketing problem, I need to hire a VP of Sales and we need to get the brand out there to grow again.' Mentions in passing: two senior people left this year, every quote over $25k still crosses Dana's desk, and 'cash has felt tight even though we're busier than ever.'
- financials_snapshot.xlsx — 3-year P&L summary plus balance-sheet/cash highlights. Revenue: $15.4M → $16.9M → $18.1M (up). Gross margin: 38% → 33% → 29% (down). Operating profit thinning; DSO stretched from 42 to 71 days; line of credit near its limit; one customer is now 31% of revenue.
- org_chart.pdf — 42-person chart. Dana sits at the hub: sales, ops, purchasing, and finance all report directly to the owner; the two roles that left (Ops Manager, Controller) are shown 'vacant / covered by Dana.'
- firm_bench_roster.md — available C-suite consultants (fractional CFO, COO, CMO, CHRO, CIO/CTO) with day rates and short bios, plus two strategic-alliance partner firms (one restructuring/turnaround boutique, one go-to-market agency).
- crm_pipeline_card.md — partial CRM entry: Source = referral (warm); Stage = Discovery; Engagement model = [blank]; Commercial terms / revenue % = [blank]; Next step = [blank]; Decision-maker = Dana (sole owner).
- inbound_email.md — the referrer's intro plus Dana's follow-up: 'Really enjoyed the call. Send me a proposal for how you'd help us grow — and what it costs.'
tasks: 1) Diagnosis memo (≤1 page). Working from the transcript, financials, and org chart together, name the 2-3 CORE issues at Meridian (root causes, in your own peer-level read — not necessarily the problem Dana named), and briefly say what evidence in the materials points to each. Then list the 3-5 questions you would put to Dana in the next conversation BEFORE proposing any solution.

2) Engagement design (≤1 page). Recommend the engagement model (fractional vs. interim vs. project-based) and why it fits THIS situation; the scope and first-90-day focus; the engagement team you would assemble — which existing Meridian staff to lean on, which firm-bench C-suite role(s) to pull in, and whether to bring an alliance partner — with a one-line reason for each pick; and the 2-3 success metrics you would commit to.

3) Win the deal. Draft the follow-up note to Dana that moves this from Discovery toward a signed engagement (her email asked for a 'proposal to help us grow, and what it costs'). Then state how you would structure the commercial terms given the firm's revenue-share / no-base model and Meridian's cash situation, and write a 3-line CRM pipeline update (stage, next step, top risk).

4) DECISIONS log. A short bulleted list covering every open call you had to make (engagement model, team composition, success metrics, commercial structure, and how literally you took Dana's 'we need to grow' framing): for each — what you chose, the alternative you rejected and why, and the one thing you'd confirm with Dana or with the firm before committing.

coverProbes.where: discovery_call_transcript.md (Dana's 'sales & marketing problem, hire a VP of Sales' framing) read against financials_snapshot.xlsx (margin erosion, stretched DSO, maxed credit line, 31% customer concentration) and org_chart.pdf (owner-as-bottleneck, two senior vacancies).
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate reads the financials and org chart before accepting the founder's framing, and reframes the engagement around margin/cash and owner-dependency rather than the lead-gen story Dana told. A naive one-shot response takes 'we need to grow / hire a sales VP' at face value and proposes a go-to-market push — selling the client what they asked for instead of what the evidence shows they need.
decisionSpace: Accept Dana's framing and scope a growth/go-market engagement (honors the client's stated ask and the warm relationship, but risks treating a symptom).

Reframe as a margin-recovery + reduce-owner-dependency engagement and gently challenge the framing on the next call (higher diagnostic integrity, but risks friction with an owner who may not want to hear it).
Sequence it: stabilize margin/cash and offload decisions from Dana first, then revisit growth once the base is sound (defensible middle path, but slower to the revenue Dana is impatient for).

coverProbes.where: financials_snapshot.xlsx — top line rising ($15.4M→$18.1M) while gross margin (38%→29%), DSO (42→71), and the credit line all deteriorate.
coverProbes.reveals: A careful candidate verifies the trend beneath the rising top line and recognizes that scaling negative-trending unit economics burns cash faster — so 'they're growing, recommend a scaling engagement + a CMO' is subtly wrong even though it passes a shallow 'is revenue up?' check. A naive response anchors on the growing revenue and recommends scaling.
decisionSpace: Scale now and fix the economics in parallel (fastest to upside, but bets the company's tight cash on doing two hard things at once).
Pause scaling and fix margin + cash collection first (protects survival, but tells an impatient owner to slow down).
Selective growth in the profitable segment only while shrinking or repricing the dilutive/concentrated business (targeted, but operationally harder and needs data the packet doesn't fully provide).

coverProbes.where: crm_pipeline_card.md (Engagement model and Commercial terms / revenue % both blank) plus the firm's stated revenue-share, no-base model and Meridian's near-maxed credit line.
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate flags that the engagement model and the core commercial term are undefined, proposes a structure tied to the engagement type and the client's cash constraint, and notes what must be confirmed with the firm. A naive response either invents a fee with no rationale or quietly ignores the gap.
decisionSpace: Fixed monthly retainer (predictable income, simple to sell, but caps upside and leans on the client's scarce cash).

Reduced retainer + outcome fee tied to margin/EBITDA or cash improvement (aligns incentives and eases near-term cash, but carries real income risk under a no-base model and needs a clean measurement baseline).
Scoped project fee for a 90-day diagnostic-to-plan, then re-contract for delivery (de-risks both sides and earns trust first, but defers the larger engagement and revenue).

coverProbes.where: No success metrics are defined anywhere in the packet; Task 2 forces the candidate to commit to 2-3.
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate ties metrics to the real root cause (gross margin %, cash/DSO, decisions delegated off the owner, leadership-bench capability) and makes them measurable against today's baseline. A naive response defaults to vanity top-line growth — the very framing the financials undercut.
decisionSpace: Financial metrics (gross-margin recovery, cash runway / DSO) — directly tied to survival, but may feel narrow to an owner chasing growth.

Organizational metrics (decisions removed from Dana's desk, key vacancies filled, a functioning leadership team) — addresses the bottleneck and the team-building mandate, but harder to quantify and slower to show.
A small balanced set spanning both, with one leading and one lagging indicator (most complete, but risks over-instrumenting a 90-day start).
